newsitem.title: USA: Clinton claims credit for cutting deficit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton claims credit for cutting deficit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday claimed election-year credit for new figures showing a further decline in the U.S. budget deficit, saying it was evidence his economic policies were working.

Taking a jab at Republican Bob Dole's appeal to Americans to "wake up" and reject Clinton on Election Day Nov. 5, the president told a rousing campaign rally in this St. Louis suburb: "I would say that these results prove that America is awake and moving in the right direction."

Republicans contended Clinton deserved no credit because they had to drag him into making reductions in government spending after they took control of Congress two years ago. Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici of New Mexico said the lower deficit "vindicates our willingness to stand up to Bill Clinton."

But Clinton staked claim to credit on his visit to the "Show Me" state, nicknamed for Missourians' reputation for requiring proof of claims. On the steps of city hall he stood in front of a large chart showing the country's red-ink spending was $290 billion in 1992 when he was elected and had declined every year he has been in office.

Two teens joined him on stage to pull a string unveiling the deficit figure for the 1996 budget year that ends Oct. 31 was $107 billion, the lowest budget deficit in 15 years, since 1981, Republican Ronald Reagan's first year as president.
Clinton said he was the first 20th century president to see the deficit decline in all four years of his term and had more than fulfilled a 1992 pledge to cut the deficit in half.

If not for deficit-spending under Reagan and his Republican successor George Bush, he asserted, the budget would be in surplus. "We all know that our budget would be in surplus today if it weren't for the interest we pay on the debt rung up in the 12 years before I took office," he said.

Franklin Raines, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which compiles the figure, said the drop reflected both stronger-than-expected growth that raised tax revenue and efforts to control government spending.
"About half is from the increase in economic growth and about half is from holding down spending," he told reporters on the third stop on a three-day, seven-state campaign trip.
To the Republican argument that the spending reductions they pushed were responsible for the favourable news, Raines argued that Republican contribution had been limited.

"The spending reductions since the Republican majority has been in place have been relatively modest compared to the overall total," he said. "Although we have been able work with them in the last year on the mutually acceptable budget ... if we had been able to do (that) earlier these numbers could have been much better."

Raines also said he expected the fiscal year 1997 budget deficit to be lower than the $144 billion that OMB estimated in March, largely because growth was likely to be stronger than was then expected.

Clinton was to make speeches in Minneapolis and Chicago on Monday and in Columbus, Ohio and Chicago on Tuesday, before returning to the White House for a one-night stopover. He leaves on Wednesday for his final, seven-day campaign blitz that will culminate in Little Rock, Arkansas, where he will spend election night.
